label: Wed 4 Nov · midday (first edition)
window: Tue 3 Nov evening → Wed 4 Nov midday (Warsaw time), with key events from Mon–Tue
bigPicture: The US midterm elections handed both houses of Congress to the Democrats, and the world's markets spent the night repricing: Asian tech shares plunged then recovered, the dollar fell to a one-month low (lifting the złoty), European banks and wind-power firms jumped, and gold rose about 3%. Strong results from chipmaker AMD calmed some fears of an AI bubble, while China is struggling to stop a stock-market slide. Underneath it all, the US–Iran conflict around the Strait of Hormuz keeps oil above $100, pushing central banks from Australia to Sweden to raise interest rates, and Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's power grid as winter approaches.

stories.rankWhy: The world's largest economy changed who controls its laws and budget; it moved the dollar, gold, bonds and shares on every continent within hours.
stories.title: Democrats win control of both the US House and Senate
stories.what: In Tuesday's US midterm elections the Democratic Party won majorities in both chambers of Congress, flipping Senate seats in states including Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. President Trump (Republican) stays in office until 2029 but now faces a Congress run by the other party. Flipping both chambers in a midterm has happened only a handful of times since World War II.
stories.why: Congress writes US laws and approves spending. An opposition Congress can block the president's plans, launch investigations and shape rules on things markets care about, such as AI regulation, defence budgets and clean energy. Because the dollar is the world's main currency, shifts in Washington ripple everywhere.
stories.everyday: No new law exists yet, but expectations changed, and that alone moved currencies, share prices and gold, including the value of the złoty in your wallet.

stories.rankWhy: Hormuz carried about a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the war; its partial closure sets fuel, heating and inflation costs for billions of people.
stories.title: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as oil stays above $100
stories.what: On Monday the US military carried out what officials called limited, defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, the largest island in the Persian Gulf, after Iran fired on US aircraft. It was the first US attack on the island since June. The US–Iran war began on 28 February and has sharply cut shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar is mediating; the US Vice President said he hopes for a negotiated settlement, while Iran says its conditions must be met before Hormuz reopens.
stories.why: When a chokepoint like Hormuz is blocked, supply shrinks and prices rise everywhere. Brent crude, the global benchmark, is around $103 a barrel, roughly 60% higher than a year ago. Every hint of peace pushes oil down, every strike pushes it up: traders call that extra price the 'risk premium'. High oil is now the main reason many central banks are raising interest rates.
stories.everyday: Oil feeds into petrol, diesel, heating, plastics, transport and food costs, so it shows up in prices in Polish shops too.

stories.rankWhy: The dollar is used in most world trade and debt; when it moves, every other currency, commodity and emerging market feels it.
stories.title: The US dollar slides to a one-month low
stories.what: The dollar weakened against most major currencies after the election results: the euro rose to about $1.123 and the yen strengthened slightly. US government bond yields (the interest the US pays to borrow) also fell.
stories.why: Investors expect a divided Washington to mean less new government spending and possibly lower US interest rates in future. Lower expected US rates make dollar savings less attractive, so money flows elsewhere. A weaker dollar makes dollar-priced goods like oil and gold cheaper for everyone else, and eases pressure on countries that borrowed in dollars.
stories.everyday: For someone in Poland, a weaker dollar means dollar-priced things (fuel on world markets, many electronics, travel to the US) get a bit cheaper in złoty.

stories.rankWhy: Asia's chip and AI companies supply the whole world's tech industry; a near-5% swing in Tokyo signals how fragile global AI-related share prices are.
stories.title: Tokyo's stock market plunges almost 5%, then recovers most of the fall
stories.what: Japan's Nikkei 225 fell as much as 4.8% on Wednesday as investors feared a Democratic Congress could bring tighter AI rules; chip and AI-related shares fell hardest. It then recovered to close about 1.4% lower. South Korea's Kospi reversed an early drop of more than 3% to end higher, and Hong Kong and Shanghai rose.
stories.why: Asia trades while Europe and the US sleep, so it reacts first to overnight US news. Japan, Korea and Taiwan host many of the companies that make AI chips and parts, so fear of slower AI spending hits them hardest. The swing shows how nervous investors already were after weeks of worry that AI shares had become too expensive.
stories.everyday: Pension and investment funds hold these shares, but one-day swings like this rarely matter for long-term savers.

stories.rankWhy: AMD is a ~$750bn chip giant and a bellwether for AI spending; its results moved chip shares worldwide and eased AI-bubble fears.
stories.title: AMD's AI chip sales nearly double, calming some AI-bubble fears
stories.what: US chipmaker AMD reported third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier. Its data-centre business, which sells server processors and AI chips to cloud companies, rose 97% to a record $8.5 billion. It forecast about $17 billion in revenue next quarter, above expectations, and its shares rose around 8% in after-hours trading after falling more than 20% in the previous month.
stories.why: Investors have been asking whether the huge spending on AI will pay off. Strong sales at a major supplier suggest demand is still real, which is why chip stocks in Europe and Asia found buyers on Wednesday. One company's earnings report can move a whole sector when it acts as a signal for the industry.
stories.everyday: AI data centres drive demand for chips, electricity and buildings worldwide, which affects jobs, energy prices and tech prices.

stories.rankWhy: China is the world's second-largest economy and stock market; whether Beijing can stop the slide affects global growth, commodities and Asian markets.
stories.title: China revives its stock-market rescue tools, but investors stay sceptical
stories.what: After China's main CSI 300 index fell 8.5% in October, its worst month since early 2016, Beijing brought back support tools first used in 2024: cheap central-bank funding for brokers and insurers to buy shares, and cheaper loans for companies to buy back their own shares. The tech-heavy Star 50 index still fell 3.8% on Tuesday, though Shanghai shares rose about 1.9% on Wednesday.
stories.why: Unlike in 2024, the tools came without an interest-rate cut, so many investors doubt they're enough. China's problems run deeper: a long property crisis and weak consumer spending. When governments prop up markets, prices may hold for a while, but lasting gains usually need company profits to improve.
stories.everyday: A weaker Chinese economy buys fewer raw materials and machines from abroad, including from European and Polish exporters.

stories.rankWhy: Ends a decades-old pillar of US Middle East policy during an active regional war; affects defence companies and the region's security balance.
stories.title: Trump says US military aid to Israel will end this year
stories.what: President Trump said the US will stop its roughly $4 billion a year in military aid to Israel at the end of 2026, saying Prime Minister Netanyahu raised the idea. The current 10-year agreement, worth about $3.8 billion a year, was due to run until 2028. Israel will still be able to buy US weapons with its own money.
stories.why: Most of this aid was spent on American-made weapons, so it also mattered to US defence companies. Ending it early changes Israel's budget and could shift how the region's security is financed, at a time when the Middle East is already at war. Some in Congress urged a gradual phase-out instead.
stories.everyday: Defence spending decisions affect government budgets and the defence industry, which employs many people in the US and Europe.

stories.rankWhy: Europe's biggest war: attacks on Ukraine's grid before winter affect millions of people, European energy markets and next week's peace talks.
stories.title: Russia strikes Ukraine's power stations as temperatures fall
stories.what: Russia said it hit two power stations in Ukraine's Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions, after missile and drone attacks on Tuesday cut electricity to large parts of Ukraine. In Zhytomyr region alone more than 180,000 customers lost power. The strikes came a week before US-brokered peace talks are due to resume.
stories.why: Hitting energy systems before winter puts pressure on civilians and on Ukraine's economy, and damages factories that need power. The war also shapes Europe's energy security, defence spending and refugee flows. Any progress or collapse in peace talks would move European gas prices, defence shares and the currencies of neighbouring countries.
stories.everyday: Poland borders Ukraine: the war affects Polish defence spending, energy policy, trade and the many Ukrainians living in Poland.

stories.rankWhy: Big moves across whole sectors of Europe's stock market, but no lasting change to the economy yet.
stories.title: Same news, different winners: European banks and wind power rise, defence falls
stories.what: European shares opened nervously but turned higher. Banks led: Deutsche Bank rose about 3.6%, and Intesa Sanpaolo, Commerzbank, Société Générale, Santander and UniCredit around 3%. Danish wind-farm developer Ørsted jumped about 7% and turbine maker Vestas about 5%. Defence companies fell.
stories.why: One event affects sectors differently. Clean-energy firms had struggled under current US policies, so investors bet a Democratic Congress will be friendlier. Defence firms that sell to the US military fell on fears that US military spending might grow more slowly. By late morning Germany's DAX was up about 1.3% and Spain's IBEX about 2.3%.
stories.everyday: Share prices move on forecasts about the future, not just on today's profits.

stories.rankWhy: Directly affects prices, loans and savings for 37 million Poles, but has little effect outside Poland.
stories.title: The złoty strengthens as the dollar falls
stories.what: The złoty gained against the dollar on Wednesday morning (USD/PLN fell about 0.5%), and the euro slipped back to around 4.40–4.41 zł. Late last week the euro had briefly cost the most złoty since November 2023, as a domestic political dispute over Poland's Constitutional Tribunal weighed on the currency. The WIG20 index rose about 0.5%.
stories.why: Exchange rates are relative: when the dollar weakens worldwide, the złoty looks stronger against it. Domestic politics matter too, because investors want stable institutions in the countries where they keep money. A weaker dollar generally helps emerging markets like Poland, as global investors look beyond the US.
stories.everyday: A stronger złoty makes imports, foreign holidays and dollar-priced fuel cheaper; a weaker one helps Polish exporters selling abroad.

stories.rankWhy: Raises loan costs for millions of Australian households and confirms a worldwide trend of rate hikes driven by oil, but Australia alone moves few global markets.
stories.title: Australia raises interest rates for the fifth time this year
stories.what: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its main rate (the 'cash rate') by 0.25 percentage points to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote. It cited stubborn inflation, the Middle East war and high oil prices. Australia's big four banks will raise mortgage rates from 13 November.
stories.why: Central banks raise rates to cool inflation: borrowing gets more expensive, people and companies spend less, and price rises slow. The split vote and softer wording hint at a pause in December, so the Australian dollar actually fell. Markets react not only to what a central bank does, but to hints about what it will do next.
stories.everyday: The same mechanism works in Poland: when the NBP changes rates, monthly loan payments for millions of households change too.

stories.rankWhy: Part of the same global wave of rate rises caused by energy prices; important for Sweden and a signal for other European central banks.
stories.title: Sweden raises interest rates for the first time since 2023
stories.what: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, raised its key rate from 1.75% to 2.00% on Wednesday, as all economists surveyed had expected. It is the bank's first hike since 2023, driven by the risk that higher energy prices spread into wider inflation.
stories.why: Two central banks on opposite sides of the world raising rates in two days shows the oil shock turning into a global inflation problem. When many central banks tighten at once, borrowing gets more expensive worldwide and economic growth tends to slow.
stories.everyday: If inflation from energy spreads in Europe, the NBP could also face pressure to keep Polish rates higher for longer.

stories.rankWhy: A big daily move in a key safe-haven asset that central banks hold, but a reaction to other news rather than a cause.
stories.title: Gold jumps about 3% to roughly $4,050 an ounce
stories.what: Gold futures rose almost 3% on Wednesday to around $4,050 per troy ounce as the dollar weakened and investors sought protection amid political and geopolitical uncertainty.
stories.why: Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar makes it cheaper for everyone else and demand rises. It's also a 'safe haven': when the future feels uncertain, some people move money into it because it can't go bankrupt or be printed by a government.
stories.everyday: Gold affects jewellery prices and the value of reserves held by central banks; the NBP has been one of the world's biggest gold buyers in recent years.

stories.rankWhy: Novo Nordisk is one of Europe's most valuable companies and central to Denmark's economy; good for its shareholders and patients, limited wider effect.
stories.title: Novo Nordisk jumps on strong sales of its Wegovy weight-loss pill
stories.what: Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk raised its 2026 outlook after third-quarter results beat expectations. Sales of its new Wegovy pill reached 5.4 billion Danish kroner versus about 4.5 billion expected. Its shares jumped as much as about 6% but are still down roughly 17% this year, as US rival Eli Lilly has overtaken it in the biggest market.
stories.why: Results that beat analysts' forecasts usually lift a share price, because the price already contains the forecast. Novo also plans price cuts in the US and its finance chief is leaving, showing how competition squeezes even very successful products.
stories.everyday: Weight-loss drugs are reshaping healthcare spending and even food companies' sales in many countries.

stories.rankWhy: A deal would ease a costly tariff war between two of the world's most connected economies; not yet agreed.
stories.title: US and Canada say a trade deal is getting closer
stories.what: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said negotiations with the US have become 'more intense' after a call with President Trump, who said the two sides have 'the concept' of a deal. Since talks broke down in August, the US has applied 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, and Canada has retaliated.
stories.why: Tariffs are taxes on imports. They raise costs for businesses that rely on parts crossing the border, especially car and steel makers. Canada sends more than 90% of its crude oil to the US, so the two economies are tightly linked. A deal could lower costs and lift shares of companies hurt by the trade war.
stories.everyday: Trade wars push up prices for consumers on both sides; the same mechanism affects EU exporters facing US tariffs.

stories.rankWhy: Hit food retailers in at least 11 countries and triggered EU-level alarm, but the damage so far is limited to some stores.
stories.title: Hackers switch off supermarket freezers across Europe
stories.what: Cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems have hit stores in at least 11 European countries in recent days, including Belgium, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany (four stores), Romania (six) and the UK. Shops had to throw away spoiled food. Italy held emergency talks with its intelligence chiefs. No group has claimed responsibility; Romania's cyber chief called the attacks semi-amateurish and said he doesn't suspect a state.
stories.why: Many machines in shops and factories are now connected to the internet, and old, poorly protected systems are easy targets. Attacks on food supply chains raise costs for retailers and insurers and push companies and governments to spend more on cybersecurity.
stories.everyday: Cyberattacks can empty shelves locally and eventually raise prices if firms must pay more for security and insurance.

stories.rankWhy: Disrupted air travel in several countries, including a Warsaw-area airport; no devices found and little market impact so far.
stories.title: Bomb threats hit at least seven European flights, including two to Warsaw
stories.what: At least seven passenger flights in Europe received bomb threats on Tuesday, including two flights to Warsaw, two to Sofia, two to Rome and one to Murcia in Spain, and an Israel-bound cruise ship was searched in Greece. An airport near Warsaw was briefly shut, and Italy's air force escorted one plane into Rome. No explosives were found.
stories.why: Even hoax threats cost airlines money through delays, diversions and security checks, and they test how well countries respond. Experts say such low-cost, hard-to-trace disruption is becoming more common; authorities are investigating whether the incidents are linked.
stories.everyday: If threats continue, travellers can expect more delays and tighter security checks at airports.

stories.rankWhy: Bangladesh is the world's second-largest clothing exporter; strikes there can delay supplies and raise costs for global fashion brands.
stories.title: Bangladesh garment workers protest for a fifth day over pay
stories.what: Garment workers in Bangladesh are protesting for higher pay as living costs rise, demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (about $243), more than double the current 12,500. At one point unrest shut 529 factories and left nearly a million workers idle. A new wage board of government, worker and employer representatives held its first meeting on Wednesday as clashes continued.
stories.why: Clothing makes up about 10% of Bangladesh's economy and most of its export earnings. Higher wages help workers cope with inflation but raise costs for factories that compete with Vietnam, Cambodia and India. Delays can ripple to clothing brands and shops in Europe and the US.
stories.everyday: Many clothes sold in Polish shops are made in Bangladesh; supply problems there can affect prices and availability.

stories.rankWhy: Decides who governs a country at the centre of a regional war; little direct market effect yet.
stories.title: Israel's election commission finds no fraud as coalition talks begin
stories.what: Israel's election commission said it found no evidence of fraud in last week's vote, rejecting claims by Prime Minister Netanyahu and his allies. Neither Netanyahu's bloc (53 seats) nor rival Gadi Eisenkot's (48) has the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat parliament. President Herzog now consults the parties; if no one can form a government, Israel could hold another election early next year.
stories.why: Who governs Israel affects the wars in the region, relations with the US and Arab states, and Israel's economy. Long political deadlock can delay budgets and decisions, which investors dislike.
stories.everyday: Middle East stability feeds into oil prices and the risk of wider conflict.

stories.rankWhy: Shapes the EU's future farm market and directly concerns Polish farmers; a long negotiation, not an immediate shock.
stories.title: Ukraine says EU limits on its farm exports must be temporary
stories.what: Ukraine's Prime Minister told a Euronews summit that any EU restrictions on Ukrainian wheat and grain after it joins the EU must be temporary, with clear exit conditions. Ukraine is now one of four 'frontrunner' candidates, with Montenegro, Albania and Moldova, and the European Commission is publishing a roadmap for them. Armenia's leader said applying for EU membership in 2027 or 2028 is realistic.
stories.why: Ukraine is one of the world's biggest grain exporters. Letting its farm goods into the EU freely would lower food prices but pressure farmers in neighbouring countries, which is why some EU members want limits. Joining the EU is a long process that reshapes trade, investment and budgets.
stories.everyday: Polish farmers protested against Ukrainian grain imports in 2024, so these talks matter directly for Polish agriculture and food prices.

stories.rankWhy: Strong results at Italy's biggest bank; good for its shareholders, little wider effect.
stories.title: Italy's biggest bank posts record profit
stories.what: Intesa Sanpaolo reported a record €8.2 billion net profit for the first nine months of 2026, up about 8%, and now expects 'well above' €10 billion for the full year. It will pay a €3.8 billion interim dividend on 25 November.
stories.why: Banks earn more when interest rates are relatively high, because the gap between what they charge borrowers and pay savers widens. Strong bank profits also mean more dividends and taxes, though Italy's budget law took about €0.9 billion from Intesa this year.
stories.everyday: Bank profits depend partly on the interest you pay on loans and receive on deposits.

stories.rankWhy: A solid day for one of the world's largest stock markets, but no big shift.
stories.title: India's stock market rises for a fifth day in a row
stories.what: India's Sensex rose 0.5% to 77,301 and the Nifty 50 gained 0.6% to 23,961 on Wednesday, the fifth straight day of gains, led by consumer, property and metal shares. IT companies fell more than 1%.
stories.why: India is one of the fastest-growing big economies, and foreign investors watch it as an alternative to China. IT shares fell because many Indian IT firms earn their money from US clients, so worries about US tech spending hit them.
stories.everyday: Many global and Polish investment funds hold Indian shares as part of 'emerging markets' funds.

stories.rankWhy: Notable moves for Latin American currencies and Argentina's borrowing costs, but regional in scope.
stories.title: Argentina's borrowing risk hits a one-year high; Latin American currencies slip
stories.what: Argentina's 'country risk', the extra interest investors demand to hold its dollar bonds, rose to about 829 points on Tuesday, its highest in a year, and the Buenos Aires Merval index fell roughly 2–3%. The Brazilian real and the Mexican and Colombian pesos each lost more than 1% against the dollar. Brazil's central bank announces a rate decision on Wednesday evening and Mexico's on Thursday.
stories.why: When investors see a country as riskier, it must pay more to borrow, which squeezes its government and businesses. Latin American currencies often move together because global investors treat the region as one group.
stories.everyday: Country risk is like a credit score for a whole country: a worse score means more expensive loans for everyone there.

stories.rankWhy: Shows the other side of the oil shock for Africa's most populous country; small effect on world markets.
stories.title: High oil prices help Nigeria's currency and reserves
stories.what: Nigeria's naira has held steady around ₦1,347 per dollar, supported by its oil, Bonny Light, selling at about $115 a barrel and oil output at a four-year high. Foreign-exchange reserves rose to about $55 billion.
stories.why: The same oil shock that hurts importers like Poland helps exporters like Nigeria: more dollars flow in, which supports the currency and lets the central bank defend it. It's a reminder that every price change creates winners and losers.
stories.everyday: In Nigeria, a steadier naira helps keep the price of imported goods under control, although petrol is still expected to get more expensive.

stories.rankWhy: Diplomatic signal from the world's largest oil importer; no concrete effect yet.
stories.title: China steps up Middle East diplomacy
stories.what: China said avoiding new hostilities in the Middle East is a 'top priority' and announced it will send three senior envoys to seven countries across the Middle East and Africa.
stories.why: China is the world's largest crude-oil buyer, much of it from the Gulf, so a blocked Hormuz hurts its economy directly. Energy needs shape foreign policy. If more big powers press for calm, oil prices could ease.
stories.everyday: Calmer energy markets would mean lower fuel and heating costs worldwide.

stories.rankWhy: A long-running territorial dispute over busy shipping lanes; diplomacy continues, no new escalation.
stories.title: Philippines and China promise to keep talking despite sea dispute
stories.what: The foreign ministers of the Philippines and China agreed to maintain dialogue after a tense call, though China accused some Philippine politicians of crossing its 'red lines'. Leaders are due to meet at the ASEAN summit in Manila and APEC meetings in Shenzhen later this month.
stories.why: The South China Sea carries a huge share of world shipping and may hold gas reserves. Calm relations reduce the risk of incidents that could disrupt trade routes.
stories.everyday: Many goods sold in Europe travel through these waters, so stability there helps keep shipping costs down.

stories.rankWhy: A voluntary plan, not a binding rule; sets the agenda for next week's COP31 climate summit.
stories.title: Brazil publishes the first global roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels
stories.what: Brazil, which hosted last year's COP30 climate summit, published a voluntary roadmap for countries to shift away from oil, gas and coal, with national plans by 2028 and the main cuts to fossil-fuel production expected from 2031 to 2033. It will be discussed at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November.
stories.why: The energy transition will reshape which industries and countries grow over the next decades. Roadmaps like this influence where investors put money, from oil fields to wind farms, even when they aren't binding.
stories.everyday: Climate policy affects energy bills, car choices and jobs, including Poland's coal-dependent regions.

stories.rankWhy: Local elections in Africa's most industrialised economy; matters for confidence in South Africa, little global effect.
stories.title: South Africans vote in local elections that test the ANC
stories.what: South Africa held municipal elections on Wednesday, seen as a test for the African National Congress, the party that led the country out of white minority rule, whose support has been falling. Failing water and electricity services in many cities are central issues.
stories.why: How well cities deliver water and power affects businesses, jobs and investor confidence in South Africa, and local coalitions shape how infrastructure gets fixed.
stories.everyday: Unreliable power and water make daily life and business harder, which is why they often decide elections.

stories.rankWhy: Raises the risk of renewed conflict in a region important for fertiliser supplies; no immediate market effect.
stories.title: UN begins pulling its peacekeepers out of Western Sahara
stories.what: The UN has started preparing to withdraw its 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara after the US and Russia vetoed each other's proposals to extend it. Morocco controls most of the territory, while the Polisario Front wants independence. The UN Secretary-General warned of the risk of renewed fighting.
stories.why: It shows how disagreement between big powers at the UN can end long-running peace arrangements. Morocco is one of the world's biggest phosphate exporters, a key fertiliser ingredient, so instability there could affect global food costs.
stories.everyday: Fertiliser prices feed into the cost of growing food everywhere, including on Polish farms.

stories.rankWhy: A domestic political setback with no measurable market effect.
stories.title: Spain's transport minister resigns after deadly train crashes
stories.what: Spain's transport minister quit following deadly rail crashes, costing Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez a key ally ahead of difficult votes.
stories.why: Resignations can weaken a government's ability to pass laws and budgets; investors watch government stability because it affects public spending and borrowing.
stories.everyday: Rail safety and reliability affect millions of daily commuters.

stories.rankWhy: A long-term political ambition with no economic effect today.
stories.title: Armenia eyes an EU membership application in 2027–28
stories.what: Armenia's Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said formally applying to join the EU in 2027 or 2028 is 'realistic', as the country tries to reduce its dependence on Russia. Armenia's exports to the EU have risen sharply amid Russian trade restrictions.
stories.why: It shows how the war in Ukraine is pushing countries in Russia's neighbourhood to look west, gradually changing trade routes and alliances.
stories.everyday: Little immediate effect, but over years these shifts change who trades with whom.

lesson.title: What a market is and why news moves it
lesson.intro: A market is simply any place where people who want to buy something meet people who want to sell it, and agree on a price. Today's news shows the most important idea in this whole course: prices move on expectations about the future, not only on what is happening right now.

sections.heading: Markets are everywhere
sections.body: A street market where you buy apples is a market. So is the stock exchange in Warsaw, where people buy and sell small pieces of companies, and the currency market, where banks swap złoty for euros or dollars. The ideas are the same: buyers, sellers and a price that changes until enough of them agree.

sections.heading: A price is a summary of opinions
sections.body: If many people suddenly want to buy and few want to sell, the price rises. If many want to sell, it falls. So a price is like a live vote: it sums up what millions of people think something is worth, given everything they know.

sections.heading: Why news moves prices
sections.body: News changes what people know, and so it changes what they expect will happen. When expectations change, people buy or sell, and prices move. This often happens within seconds, long before anything real changes. A factory doesn't produce less overnight because of an election, but its share price can still fall overnight if investors think future laws will hurt its profits.

sections.heading: The four markets we'll follow
sections.body: Stocks (shares in companies), currencies (the price of one money in another), commodities (raw materials like oil, gold and wheat) and interest rates or bonds (the price of borrowing money). They are all connected: a war can raise oil prices, which raises inflation, which pushes a central bank to raise interest rates, which moves currencies and stocks. Tracing those chains is the skill you'll build.

lesson.todayExample: Overnight, US voters gave the Democrats control of Congress. No new law has been passed yet. But investors expect different future policies, so within hours the dollar fell, the złoty strengthened, European wind-power companies jumped about 7%, defence companies fell, and gold rose about 3%. Same news, very different moves, all driven by changed expectations.
takeaways: A market is wherever buyers and sellers agree on a price.
A price summarises what many people expect, not just what is true today.
News moves markets by changing expectations, often instantly.
Stocks, currencies, commodities and interest rates are linked, so one event can ripple across all of them.

quiz.q: Why did European defence companies' shares fall after the US election, even though nothing about their business changed overnight?
options: They had a bad quarter of profits
Investors expect US military spending might grow more slowly under a Democratic Congress
European governments cancelled orders
Defence companies always fall in November
quiz.explain: Prices move on expectations. Investors guessed future US spending could grow more slowly, so they sold before anything actually changed.

quiz.q: The dollar weakened worldwide. What happened to the złoty against the dollar?
options: It weakened too
It strengthened: one dollar now costs fewer złoty
Nothing; the złoty isn't affected by the dollar
The złoty was suspended from trading
quiz.explain: Exchange rates are relative. If the dollar falls, it buys fewer złoty, so USD/PLN goes down and the złoty looks stronger.

quiz.q: Why does a conflict around the Strait of Hormuz matter for petrol prices in Poland?
options: Poland buys all its oil from Iran
About a fifth of the world's oil and gas used to pass through it, so less supply raises prices globally
It only matters for the US
It doesn't; petrol prices are set by the Polish government
quiz.explain: Oil is traded globally. Less supply anywhere pushes up the world price (Brent), which feeds into fuel costs everywhere.

quiz.q: Australia's central bank raised interest rates. What is the main goal of doing that?
options: To make the stock market go up
To slow inflation by making borrowing more expensive
To make the Australian dollar weaker
To help people get cheaper mortgages
quiz.explain: Higher rates make loans costlier, so people and firms spend less, which eases pressure on prices.

quiz.q: Japan's Nikkei fell almost 5% during the day but closed down only 1.4%. What does this mostly show?
options: Japanese companies lost 5% of their factories
Investors first reacted with fear, then reconsidered as more information arrived
The exchange made an error
Japan's government bought all the shares
quiz.explain: Markets often overreact to surprising news and then adjust as people think it through. That's volatility in action.

glossary.def: Any place, physical or electronic, where buyers and sellers meet and agree on a price.
glossary.example: The Warsaw Stock Exchange is a market for shares in Polish companies.

glossary.def: What people believe will happen in the future. Prices change when expectations change, often before anything real happens.
glossary.example: Shares in wind-power firms rose because investors expect friendlier US policies.

glossary.def: A small piece of ownership in a company. Its price rises and falls with what investors expect the company to earn.
glossary.example: Owning one share of PKO BP means owning a tiny slice of that bank.

glossary.def: A number that tracks the combined share prices of a group of companies, used as a thermometer for a whole market.
glossary.example: The WIG20 tracks Poland's 20 biggest listed companies.

glossary.def: A group of companies in the same line of business, such as banks, energy or technology.
glossary.example: On 4 November the bank sector rose while the defence sector fell.

glossary.def: How much and how quickly a price swings up and down. High volatility means big, fast moves.
glossary.example: The Nikkei fell 4.8% and then recovered most of it in one day.

glossary.def: Rules set by governments that companies must follow. New rules can raise costs or limit what firms can do.
glossary.example: Investors worry new AI rules could slow spending on AI chips.

glossary.def: The price of one currency in another.
glossary.example: EUR/PLN at 4.40 means one euro costs 4.40 złoty.

glossary.def: The yearly return an investor gets from a bond, shown as a percentage. When bond prices rise, yields fall, and the other way round.
glossary.example: US government bond yields fell after the election.

glossary.def: Something people buy when they're worried, because they expect it to hold its value in bad times.
glossary.example: Gold and, often, the Swiss franc are classic safe havens.

glossary.def: The main global price of oil, based on oil from the North Sea. Most oil in Europe, Africa and Asia is priced off it.
glossary.example: Brent at $103 means a barrel (159 litres) costs about $103.

glossary.def: A narrow sea passage that a large share of world trade must pass through. Blocking it disrupts supply.
glossary.example: The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman.

glossary.def: The extra price buyers pay because something bad might happen, such as a war disrupting supply.
glossary.example: Oil rose after the Qeshm strikes because traders added a risk premium.

glossary.def: The institution that manages a country's money and sets its main interest rate.
glossary.example: NBP in Poland, ECB for the euro, the Fed in the US, the RBA in Australia, the Riksbank in Sweden.

glossary.def: The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year.
glossary.example: A 7% mortgage rate means paying about 7% of the loan per year in interest.

glossary.def: One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%). 25 basis points = 0.25 percentage points.
glossary.example: The RBA raised rates by 25 basis points, from 4.60% to 4.85%.

glossary.def: The general rise in prices over time, which means each złoty buys a bit less.
glossary.example: If inflation is 4%, a basket costing 100 zł last year costs about 104 zł now.

glossary.def: When central banks raise interest rates or reduce the money in the system to cool inflation.
glossary.example: Australia and Sweden both tightened policy this week.

glossary.def: Contracts to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date. Their prices are often quoted as the 'live' price of commodities and indices.
glossary.example: 'Dow futures up 700 points' means traders expected US shares to open higher.

glossary.def: A company's regular update on its sales and profits, usually every three months (a quarter).
glossary.example: AMD's earnings report showed data-centre sales nearly doubling.

glossary.def: A company's own forecast of its future sales or profits. Raising guidance usually lifts the share price.
glossary.example: Novo Nordisk raised its 2026 guidance.

glossary.def: A large building full of computers that run websites, cloud services and AI.
glossary.example: AI companies are building data centres that need huge numbers of chips and electricity.

glossary.def: When a company uses its cash to buy its own shares, which often supports the share price.
glossary.example: China is offering cheap loans to help companies buy back their shares.

glossary.def: How easily money or assets can be used or traded. Central banks 'inject liquidity' by lending money into the system.
glossary.example: China's central bank is injecting liquidity so brokers can buy shares.

glossary.def: A share of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders.
glossary.example: Intesa Sanpaolo will pay a €3.8 billion interim dividend.

glossary.def: A tax on imported goods, paid when they cross a border.
glossary.example: 50% US tariffs on some Canadian goods.

glossary.def: The chain of companies and countries involved in making and delivering a product.
glossary.example: A T-shirt might be sewn in Bangladesh, shipped via Asia and sold in Poland.

glossary.def: The extra interest investors demand to lend to a country compared with a very safe borrower like the US. Higher means riskier.
glossary.example: Argentina's country risk rose to about 829 points, its highest in a year.

glossary.def: A country whose economy is growing fast and becoming more developed, such as Poland, India or Brazil.
glossary.example: A weaker dollar often helps emerging-market currencies.

glossary.def: Foreign currency and gold a central bank holds to pay for imports, repay foreign debt and defend its own currency.
glossary.example: Nigeria's reserves rose to about $55 billion.

glossary.def: The lowest pay employers are legally allowed to pay workers.
glossary.example: Bangladeshi garment workers want the minimum wage raised to 30,000 taka.

glossary.def: An attempt to damage, disrupt or steal from computer systems.
glossary.example: Hackers raised the temperature of supermarket freezers across Europe.

glossary.def: A false warning or trick made to look real.
glossary.example: None of the bomb threats against European flights found a real bomb.

glossary.def: A government formed by several parties together because none has a majority on its own.
glossary.example: Israel's parties are negotiating to build a coalition.

glossary.def: The process of a country joining the European Union, which involves years of negotiations and law changes.
glossary.example: Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro and Albania are the 'frontrunners' for accession.

glossary.def: The shift from fossil fuels (oil, gas, coal) towards cleaner energy like wind, solar and nuclear.
glossary.example: Brazil's roadmap proposes timelines for the energy transition.

glossary.def: A US election held halfway through a president's four-year term, choosing members of Congress.
glossary.example: The 3 November 2026 vote gave Democrats both chambers.

glossary.def: The US law-making body, with two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. It passes laws and approves spending.
glossary.example: A president needs Congress to pass a budget.

glossary.def: How geography, power and relations between countries shape events, including trade and energy.
glossary.example: China pushing for calm in the Gulf because it imports so much oil.

glossary.def: The basic physical systems a country runs on: roads, railways, power grids, water pipes.
glossary.example: Russia is striking Ukraine's power grid.

watch: US crude-oil inventory figures today at 16:30 Warsaw time; they can move oil prices.
Brazil's central bank interest-rate decision tonight; Mexico's on Thursday 5 Nov at 20:00 Warsaw time.
Bank of England interest-rate decision on Thursday.
US jobs report on Friday, a key signal for US interest rates and the dollar.
COP31 climate summit opens in Antalya on 9 Nov; US-brokered Russia–Ukraine talks resume next week.
Any progress in Qatar-led US–Iran talks: signs of reopening Hormuz would push oil lower.

moreStories.rankWhy: A fast-spreading deadly disease across several African countries, with no approved vaccine, that is already changing travel rules worldwide.
moreStories.title: Ebola outbreak becomes the fastest-growing on record, killing over 5,300
moreStories.what: An Ebola outbreak caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus has infected more than 10,000 people since May and killed about 5,376, almost all in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), according to Africa's disease-control agency. Cases have also appeared in Uganda and, for the first time, Kenya. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this strain; trials of an existing Ebola vaccine have begun. From 4 November, everyone flying to the US must sign a statement that they haven't been in the DRC in the past 21 days.
moreStories.why: The outbreak is spreading in a region hit by conflict and displacement, where people have poor access to clinics, clean water and food, which makes it hard to contain. The WHO chief says it shows why countries must finish the global pandemic treaty, which is stuck on how vaccines and tests would be shared between rich and poor countries.
moreStories.everyday: The risk in Europe is very low, but outbreaks like this can bring travel checks, strain aid budgets and remind everyone how quickly disease crosses borders.

moreStories.rankWhy: Shows Poland's growing role in European security; matters for Polish defence policy, no immediate economic effect.
moreStories.title: Poland to host the first major drills of the 'Coalition of the Willing'
moreStories.what: Poland will host the first major military exercises of the 'Coalition of the Willing', the group of mostly European countries planning security support for Ukraine, Polish media reported. Prime Minister Donald Tusk also said Poland had stopped suspicious activity on its border with Russia.
moreStories.why: Poland borders both Ukraine and Russia (through Kaliningrad), so it sits at the centre of Europe's security planning. Hosting exercises brings troops, spending and attention to Poland, and signals how seriously Europe is preparing for the region's future.
moreStories.everyday: Poland's defence spending is among the highest in NATO relative to its economy, which affects the state budget and creates jobs in the defence industry.

moreStories.rankWhy: Destructive local floods forcing hundreds to evacuate, linked to a wider pattern of extreme weather; small economic effect nationally.
moreStories.title: Flash floods sweep the US Southwest
moreStories.what: Days of heavy rain from an 'atmospheric river' (a long band of very moist air) caused flash floods across Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah, sweeping away cars and homes and forcing hundreds of people to evacuate. At least one person died. Some areas got up to five times their normal November rain; one Colorado town had to change its election-day voting plans.
moreStories.why: Extreme rain in a region that is usually in drought shows how weather is becoming more volatile. Ironically the rain helps refill reservoirs like Lake Powell that supply water to millions, though it is still lower than a year ago.
moreStories.everyday: Floods damage homes and roads and raise insurance costs, which is a growing issue in Europe too.

moreStories.rankWhy: A serious ongoing health emergency for one country, linked to a global rise in mosquito-borne disease.
moreStories.title: Dengue fever has killed 418 people in Bangladesh this year
moreStories.what: An ongoing outbreak of dengue, a disease spread by mosquitoes, has killed 418 people in Bangladesh and put more than 133,000 in hospital as of 30 October, according to health ministry data. The WHO launched new guidelines on treating dengue and similar diseases this week.
moreStories.why: Warmer temperatures and fast-growing cities are spreading mosquito-borne diseases to more places, including parts of southern Europe. Large outbreaks strain hospitals and keep people from work.
moreStories.everyday: Dengue is increasingly a concern for travellers to Asia, Africa and Latin America, and occasional local cases now appear in southern Europe.

moreStories.rankWhy: An important moment for how Britain faces its colonial past and for Caribbean demands; no economic effect for now.
moreStories.title: King Charles calls slavery 'shameful' but stops short of an apology
moreStories.what: Opening the Commonwealth summit of 56 countries in Antigua and Barbuda, King Charles III said the transatlantic slave trade fills him with horror and sorrow, but did not apologise or back reparations (compensation for historical wrongs). UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is discussing a possible formal state apology with Caribbean leaders, but has ruled out financial reparations.
moreStories.why: Caribbean and African countries argue that slavery's economic damage is still felt today and that regret alone isn't enough. How Britain responds affects its relationships across the Commonwealth.
moreStories.everyday: Debates about historical injustice shape national identity and relations between countries, as they also do in Poland regarding World War II.

moreStories.rankWhy: A serious blow to press freedom in Africa's second most populous country (about 130 million people); little direct economic effect.
moreStories.title: Ethiopia shuts down one of its last independent newspapers
moreStories.what: Ethiopia's media authority indefinitely suspended The Reporter, one of the country's oldest independent newspapers and its last privately owned Amharic-language paper, accusing it of content against 'national interests'. Human Rights Watch called on the government to reverse the decision, describing a wider crackdown on journalists.
moreStories.why: A free press lets citizens and investors find out what is really happening. Ethiopia ranks 148th of 180 countries in the press freedom index of Reporters Without Borders, and fewer independent voices make it harder to hold power to account.
moreStories.everyday: Where independent media disappear, rumours spread more easily and corruption is harder to expose.

moreStories.rankWhy: Tackles cross-border air pollution that affects the health of millions in Southeast Asia; limited global effect.
moreStories.title: Singapore toughens its law against smoke from regional forest fires
moreStories.what: After its worst haze since 2015, Singapore proposed tougher rules against companies linked to forest and land fires (mostly in Indonesia) that send smoke across borders. Offences would become arrestable, maximum fines would rise tenfold to about S$20 million, and firms could be cut off from Singapore's financial services.
moreStories.why: Fires are often set to clear land for crops like palm oil. Because the smoke crosses borders, it's hard to punish those responsible; targeting their access to finance is a new way to apply pressure.
moreStories.everyday: Palm oil is in many supermarket products sold in Europe, so how it's produced affects both the environment and people's health far away.

moreStories.rankWhy: A historic first for representation in the US; social significance rather than economic impact.
moreStories.title: The US elects its first Muslim senator
moreStories.what: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's US Senate race, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, according to the Associated Press.
moreStories.why: Milestones in representation show how a country's population and politics are changing and can shift debates on issues such as foreign policy and civil rights.
moreStories.everyday: Who sits in parliament affects which voices are heard when laws are made, in the US as in Poland.

moreStories.rankWhy: Shows the strength of tourism, a large employer worldwide, despite the oil shock; a forecast rather than a shock.
moreStories.title: World travel set for a record 1.57 billion international trips in 2026
moreStories.what: International tourist arrivals are forecast to reach a record 1.57 billion in 2026, with arrivals in Europe up about 5%, according to the WTM Global Travel Report.
moreStories.why: Tourism employs hundreds of millions of people and is a major source of income for many countries. Strong travel despite high fuel prices shows how much people prioritise it, though higher ticket prices may change where they go.
moreStories.everyday: More tourists mean more jobs in hotels and restaurants, including in Polish cities like Kraków and Gdańsk, but also busier and pricier destinations.

moreStories.rankWhy: A religious ruling with symbolic weight; very small effect on the company or markets.
moreStories.title: Libya's top religious authority tells Muslims not to wear Nike
moreStories.what: Libya's highest religious authority, Dar al-Ifta in Tripoli, issued a ruling against buying, selling or wearing Nike-branded clothing, arguing the brand's name and logo come from a Greek goddess, and repeating calls to boycott companies it sees as supporting Israel.
moreStories.why: It shows how religion and politics can affect consumer choices and global brands, though Libya is a tiny market for Nike.
moreStories.everyday: Boycotts are one way people try to influence companies with their money.

moreStories.rankWhy: A major religious event for Argentina's Catholics; no economic effect.
moreStories.title: Pope Leo XIV prepares to visit Argentina as airport workers plan a strike
moreStories.what: Pope Leo XIV is due to visit Argentina from 8 to 11 November. Two days earlier, on 6 November, a state workers' union plans a strike at 27 airports.
moreStories.why: Papal visits draw huge crowds and attention; strikes before them are a way for unions to gain leverage in a country facing economic strain.
moreStories.everyday: Airport strikes can disrupt travel for thousands of people.
